title: The Merchants of the Drowned Coast: North African Heritage in the GLMZ
body:
# The Merchants of the Drowned Coast: North African Heritage in the GLMZ

## Squeezed Between Sand and Sea

North Africa died from both directions. The Sahara came from the south. The Mediterranean came from the north. The habitable strip between them — the fertile coastal band where 200 million people had built civilizations for three thousand years — narrowed like a closing vice across the twenty-first century.

Morocco lost Casablanca to storm surge and saltwater intrusion in 2068. The city had been the economic engine of the Maghreb, a port that processed goods for all of West Africa and Southern Europe. Its flooding was not dramatic — no single catastrophic wave — but incremental, relentless. Basements flooded first. Then ground floors. Then the port infrastructure that required constant maintenance against an ocean that rose three millimeters every year, and then six, and then twelve. By 2065, the cost of maintaining Casablanca's seawalls exceeded Morocco's entire infrastructure budget. The government retreated to Marrakech, then to the Atlas Mountain foothills. Casablanca became a ruin that the ocean slowly digested.

Algiers followed a similar trajectory. The city had been built on a hillside overlooking the Mediterranean — a geography that bought it time but not salvation. The lower city flooded. The port became unusable. The hillside neighborhoods survived but lost their economic purpose when there was no port to serve. Algeria's interior was Saharan — uninhabitable without massive infrastructure investment that a collapsing state could not afford.

Tunis went under in 2074. Tripoli in 2071 — though Libya had already been a failed state for decades, and Tripoli's flooding was more a final indignity than a turning point. The Nile Delta's inundation, while technically Egyptian rather than Maghrebi, displaced 40 million people who joined the same northward and westward migration streams as their Moroccan, Algerian, and Tunisian neighbors.

By 2090, the habitable zone of North Africa had contracted to the Atlas Mountains, a handful of highland plateaus in Algeria and Tunisia, and scattered oasis communities that survived on desalination technology when they could afford it and died when they couldn't. The Sahara had advanced 300 kilometers north of its 2000 boundary. The Mediterranean had advanced between 2 and 15 kilometers inland, depending on coastal topography. An estimated 180 million people were displaced.

## The French Connection

North African migration to the GLMZ followed pathways that had been established a century earlier — not to America, but through France.

The Maghrebi diaspora in France was already the largest in Europe by 2020. Moroccan, Algerian, and Tunisian communities in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, and Lille numbered over 6 million, the legacy of colonial labor migration, postcolonial family reunification, and the persistent economic gravity of a former empire. When North Africa became uninhabitable, France was the first destination — and France, already straining under its own climate pressures and a resurgent nativist politics that made the twenty-first century's first decades look tolerant by comparison, could not absorb millions more.

The secondary migration — from France to North America — began in the 2080s and accelerated through the 2100s. Francophone Maghrebi communities settled first in Quebec, where language provided an obvious bridge. But Quebec's economy was contracting as the St. Lawrence Seaway's shipping patterns shifted, and the GLMZ corridor, growing explosively to the south, offered opportunities that Montreal could not match.

The mass driver terminal at the Lambeau Terminus processed an estimated 240,000 North African migrants between 2110 and 2150, many arriving via the Paris-to-GLMZ route that became known informally as the Barbary Express — a name the community adopted with the defiant humor of people who had been called worse.

## The Merchant Tradition

North African communities in the GLMZ gravitated toward commerce with an efficiency that reflected millennia of mercantile culture. The Phoenicians had traded from these coasts. The Carthaginians had built a commercial empire. The medieval Maghrebi merchants had operated trade networks spanning the Sahara, connecting sub-Saharan gold to Mediterranean markets. Commerce was not an occupation for North Africans in the GLMZ. It was an inheritance.

Old Harbor — the GLMZ's port district, built around the remnants of Chicago's original lakefront infrastructure — became the primary concentration point. The district's function as a trade hub aligned naturally with Maghrebi commercial instincts. North African merchants established trading houses that specialized in goods flowing through the Great Lakes shipping lanes: processed minerals from the Upper Peninsula, agricultural products from the Ironclad Agrisystems supply chain, imported goods arriving via mass driver from the Pacific Rim and European terminals.

The souk culture transplanted itself. Old Harbor's lower commercial levels — the market warrens that occupy the district's mid-grade floors — bear a visible North African architectural influence: arched passages, tessellated tilework, narrow corridors opening onto broader trading floors. These were not designed by architects following a Maghrebi aesthetic. They were built by merchants who organized commercial space the way their grandparents had, because it worked. Narrow approaches control foot traffic. Open central spaces allow shouted negotiations. Arched ceilings manage acoustics in enclosed spaces. The souk is not decorative. It is engineering refined over centuries.

Meridian Core's business districts also host a significant North African presence, particularly in the financial intermediary sector. Hawala — the informal value transfer system that predates Western banking by centuries — was adapted for the Φ economy with remarkable efficiency. North African hawala networks in the GLMZ process an estimated Φ2.3 billion annually in transfers that never touch a corponation banking system. This makes the Meridian Compact uncomfortable and Arcturus Defense Solutions' financial surveillance division very busy, but the networks persist because they serve a population that learned centuries ago not to trust institutions with their money.

## Cultural Preservation in Concrete and Steel

North African cultural preservation in the GLMZ is architectural, culinary, and linguistic — in that order of visibility.

The architectural influence extends beyond Old Harbor's souks. Riad-style interior courtyard designs appear in residential conversions throughout Old Harbor and the lower Meridian Core. In a city where exterior space is nonexistent for most residents, the North African tradition of building inward — creating private open-air spaces surrounded by living quarters — proved remarkably adaptable. Families converted standard housing units by removing interior walls and installing central light wells, creating miniature riads that brought air and light into spaces designed as sealed boxes. Building management corporations initially objected. They stopped objecting when the modifications proved to improve ventilation and reduce climate control costs.

North African cuisine — tagines, couscous, harissa, preserved lemons, mint tea — is among the most recognizable food cultures in Old Harbor. The community's culinary influence extends well beyond the ethnic population; North African spice merchants supply half the district's food vendors regardless of cuisine type.

Darija — the Moroccan Arabic dialect — and Kabyle Berber remain the community's primary heritage languages, maintained through mosque-adjacent language schools and the simple persistence of grandmothers who refuse to speak anything else to their grandchildren.

## Two Hundred Years of Intermarriage

At 2% of GLMZ genetic heritage, North African ancestry is present throughout the megacity but concentrated in Old Harbor and Meridian Core. The community's commercial networks created marriage patterns that followed trade routes rather than district boundaries — a Moroccan-descended merchant family in Old Harbor was as likely to intermarry with a Korean-descended shipping family as with another Maghrebi household, because commerce puts people in proximity regardless of origin.

Names like Benali, Bouzid, Haddad, and Amari appear across the GLMZ's surname registries, hyphenated with lineages from every continent. The community estimates its culturally active population at approximately 35,000, anchored by the mosque networks and merchant associations that serve as institutional continuity. But the genetic footprint is broader — an estimated 380,000 residents carry North African markers, many of them unaware that the spice tolerance they inherited or the commercial instinct they display traces back to merchants who once traded from a coast that the Mediterranean swallowed.
